title: The Rule of the Vital Few
subtitle: An Italian engineer found a lopsided pattern in wealth. Fifty years later, an American factory expert gave it his name — and later admitted he had stretched it.

card.essence: Twenty per cent of the causes, eighty per cent of the results. The world's favourite rule of thumb began with tax records — and the man who named it later confessed he had given Pareto too much credit.

intention: you'll learn where the 80/20 rule really comes from, use it on a small shop's problems, and practise the language of proportion: the vast majority, a handful, twice as many, hardly any.
warmup: Which small part of your week gives you most of your results — or most of your stress?
Do you wear all of your clothes, or mostly the same few? What about the apps on your phone?
In your country, is wealth shared fairly evenly, or is it very unequal?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The results were very lopsided: one team scored nine goals and the other scored none.
items.meaning: lopsided — very uneven, with much more on one side than the other.

items.sent: Every phone is checked for defects before it leaves the factory.
items.meaning: defect — a fault or problem in something that has been made.

items.sent: Only a handful of people came to the meeting — maybe six or seven.
The proportion of students who passed rose from 60% to 75%.
items.meaning: proportion — a part of a whole, often shown as a percentage or fraction.

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: rule of thumb · wealth · inequality. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) A large amount of money and possessions.
items.meaning: wealth — “Most of the family's wealth came from land.”

items.sent: (noun) An unfair situation in which some people have much more money or opportunity than others.
items.meaning: inequality — “Inequality between rich and poor areas is growing.”

items.sent: (noun) A practical, rough guide based on experience, not an exact rule.
items.meaning: rule of thumb — “As a rule of thumb, allow an hour for every ten kilometres of walking.”

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: of ___ importance  ·  check the patient's ___ signs  ·  absolutely ___
take the ___ for  ·  deserve the ___  ·  give someone ___ for an idea
items.meaning: credit — praise or recognition for something good someone has done.

items.sent: ___ food to the poor  ·  wealth is unevenly ___d  ·  ___ leaflets in the street
items.meaning: distribute — to give or share things out among people. The noun is distribution.

vocab_use: Who deserves the credit for a good idea — the person who has it, or the person who makes it famous?
What is one rule of thumb you use in daily life?
Is inequality always a problem, or only above a certain level?

story.heading: Part 1 — The engineer who counted incomes
paras: Vilfredo Pareto was born in Paris in 1848, to an Italian father and a French mother. He trained as an engineer in Turin and spent years managing railways and ironworks in Italy. He was clever, argumentative and very interested in politics — so interested that, in his forties, he changed careers completely and became an economist.

In 1893 he became a professor at the University of Lausanne, in Switzerland. There, he did something unusual for the time: instead of just arguing about how wealth should be shared, he collected numbers about how it was shared. He studied tax and income records from different countries and different centuries.

What he found surprised him. Again and again, the distribution had the same lopsided shape. A small proportion of the people had a very large share of the wealth, and the vast majority had very little. In 1896 and 1897, he published his results in a book called Cours d'économie politique.
checks: What was unusual about his method?
answers: He was an engineer (railways and ironworks).
He collected real numbers — tax and income records — instead of only arguing about how wealth should be shared.
In many countries and centuries, a small proportion of people held a very large share of the wealth.
story.discuss: Why do you think the same lopsided pattern appears in so many different countries?

story.heading: Part 2 — A legend and a number
paras: The famous version of the story says that Pareto found that 20% of the people in Italy owned 80% of the land. Many books add a charming detail: that he first noticed the pattern in his garden, when he saw that 20% of his pea plants produced 80% of the peas. There is no good evidence for the garden story. It is probably a legend added later, because it makes the idea easy to remember.
Pareto himself was interested in wealth, not in a general rule for everything. He died in 1923, long before his name became attached to the phrase “the 80/20 rule”.

That happened because of a quality expert named Joseph Juran. Born in 1904 in what is now Romania, Juran moved to the United States as a boy and grew up poor in Minnesota. He became an engineer at Western Electric, a huge telephone factory near Chicago, where he inspected products for defects.
checks: What is the famous version of Pareto's finding?
Is the pea garden story true?
Where did Juran work as a young engineer?
answers: That 20% of the people in Italy owned 80% of the land.
Probably not — there's no good evidence; it's likely a later legend.
At Western Electric, a big telephone factory near Chicago.
story.discuss: Why do legends like the pea garden spread so easily? Can you think of another one?

story.heading: Part 3 — The vital few
paras: Juran noticed that factory problems were lopsided too. A handful of causes produced the vast majority of the defects. If a factory fixed those few causes first, it could solve most of its problems quickly. In the 1940s, looking for a name for this idea, he remembered Pareto's charts of wealth and called it the Pareto principle. He described it as “the vital few and the trivial many”.

Years later, Juran admitted that he had stretched things. Pareto had never stated a universal rule; Juran had given him credit for a much bigger idea than he had actually proposed. Juran also changed his own phrase to “the vital few and the useful many”, because the “many” small causes still matter.

Today, the 80/20 rule is everywhere. Shops find that a small share of their products bring in most of their money. Software companies have found that fixing a small share of the bugs removes most of the crashes. Coaches, doctors and teachers use it too. But the numbers are a rule of thumb, not a law of nature: the real split might be 70/30 or 95/5, and the two numbers don't have to add up to 100.
checks: What did Juran notice about factory defects?
Why did Juran change “trivial many” to “useful many”?
answers: A handful of causes produced most of the defects.
Because the many small causes still matter; they aren't worthless.
No — it's a rule of thumb; the real split can be 70/30, 95/5 and so on.
story.discuss: Juran named the rule after someone who hadn't quite said it. Was that wrong, or just good marketing?

tool_tab.lead: A Pareto chart sorts causes from biggest to smallest. The bars show each cause; the red line adds them up as you go. Where the line crosses 80%, you have found your vital few. Here, 100 complaints at a small café:
how: Collect real data: complaints, faults, sales, hours — whatever you want to improve.
Group it into causes and sort from biggest to smallest.
Add the percentages as you go. Stop when you reach about 80%.
Fix those vital few first. Then look again — the chart will have changed.

sort.intro: A small online clothes shop had 200 returns last month. Which causes are the vital few (together about 80%), and which are the useful many? Add them up, then choose.

items.why: the biggest cause, 55% on its own.
8% — the third-biggest cause, but outside the top two.
only 1% — although, if the quality problem is serious, it may still deserve attention.

breaks: It's not a law. The split changes from case to case; don't force your data into 80/20.
Small causes can be serious. One rare safety problem may matter more than a hundred common annoyances.
It can be used unkindly. “Twenty per cent of customers bring eighty per cent of the profit” can lead a company to ignore everyone else.
discuss: Where would the 80/20 rule help you most — at work, at home, in your studies?
When would following the rule be a mistake?

grammar.name: quantifiers and proportions
grammar.lead: The 80/20 rule is all about how much and how many. At B2, you need a wide range of phrases to describe proportions — not only percentages.
notes:
Large parts: the (vast) majority of, most (of the), almost all (of the), nearly everyone.
“The vast majority of voters stayed at home.”  Use most without of the for general statements: “Most teenagers own a phone.”

Small parts: a (small) minority of, a handful of, a few / few, a little / little, hardly any.
“Only a handful of shops were open.”  A few = some (positive); few = not many (negative): “Few people understood the plan.”

Fractions and multiples: a quarter of, a third of, half (of) the, twice as many / much as, three times as many as.
“The new bus carries twice as many passengers as the old one.”

Agreement: the verb agrees with the noun after of.
“The majority of the money is spent on rent.”  “The majority of the students are from abroad.”

exercises.heading: Complete with one word
exercises.intro: Write one word in each gap.
items: 1. Only a ___ of people — four or five — knew the secret.
2. The vast ___ of the town's workers had jobs at the factory.
3. Our flat is small: the new one has ___ as many rooms — six instead of three.
4. There was hardly ___ food left after the party.
5. ___ people enjoy paying tax, so the government's new idea was not popular.

exercises.heading: Describe the café chart
exercises.intro: Look at the café chart in The Tool tab. Complete each sentence.
items: 1. Slow service caused ___ of all the complaints. (a fraction)
2. Cold food caused ___ as many complaints as noise. (a multiple — roughly)
3. ___ of the complaints were about Wi-Fi. (a small part — a phrase)
4. Together, two causes were responsible for the ___ of complaints. (a large part)
answers: 3. Only a few / A small minority / Hardly any

grammar.closing: Now describe your own week in proportions: what takes up the majority of your time, and what gets hardly any?

speak.intro: Look for the vital few in your own life. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “The vast majority of my … comes from …” · “Only a handful of … really matter.” · “I spend twice as much time on … as on …” · “Hardly any of …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Your vital few
paras: Which few activities give you most of your results — at work, in study, or in your health? Which give you almost nothing?

tasks.label: Task 2 — Your problems
paras: Think of something that often goes wrong for you. Are most of the problems caused by a few causes? Which ones?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Is it fair?
paras: Choose a place where a few people have most of something, such as money, attention or power. Is that a problem? Why?

final: If 20% of your friends give you 80% of your happiness, should you spend less time with the rest?
Pareto studied inequality; Juran used his name for efficiency. Is it strange that the same rule describes both?
Can a rule of thumb be useful even when it isn't exactly true?
